title: EMERGENCY FUND: HOW MUCH?
series_label: EMERGENCY FUND SIZING: 5 THINGS TO KNOW

concepts.title: Why Not 3–6 Months
concepts.body: The 3–6 month rule is a population average, not your number. 45% of Americans can't cover 3 months of expenses — flat for two years. Your target depends on job type, income stability, and dependents. One formula, four answers.

visual_spec.callout_text: 45% of Americans can't cover 3 months of expenses (Fed SHED 2025, published 2026). 30% can't cover it by any means.

concepts.title: The Formula
concepts.body: Emergency fund = essential monthly expenses × target months. Essentials only: rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, minimum debt payments, transportation. Not your income. Not your total spending. The cheapest number wins.

concepts.title: Pick Your Months
concepts.body: FDIC baseline is 3–6 months. Dual income, both stable, low fixed costs → 3 months. Single stable income or dependents → 6 months. Self-employed, commission, or contract work → 9–12 months (industry consensus above FDIC baseline). Add 1–2 months if you have heavy fixed costs or a niche job.

concepts.title: Where to Park It
concepts.body: High-yield savings account, not checking, not investing. Today's top HYSAs pay 4.20–4.50% APY (up to 5.00% intro at some banks) — a real yield, FDIC-insured, liquid in 1 day. PCE inflation is 2.7% (Fed FOMC March 2026), so your fund actually grows above inflation while it sits.

left_points: Investing can drop 30%+ in a year

concepts.title: Build It in 3 Steps
concepts.body: Step 1: Save one month of essentials first — your starter fund. Step 2: Automate weekly transfers to a separate HYSA. Step 3: Once the starter is hit, raise contributions until you reach your target. Don't invest the fund. Don't touch it for lifestyle.

sources_footer: Sourced from Federal Reserve SHED 2025 (published 2026), Fed FOMC PCE March 2026, FDIC Money Smart, Bankrate weekly
